When the year's teaching was done, Adams escaped westward, and on the slope of Long's Peak fell, by happy accident, into the arms of Clarence King — geologist, wit, and ideal American — whose friendship, begun in a one-cabin Estes Park, would last as long as either lived.

CHAPTER XXI

TWENTY YEARS AFTER (1892)

Once more! this is a story of education, not of adventure. It is meant to help young men—such as have intelligence enough to seek help—but not to amuse them. What one did—or did not do—with one's education, after getting it, concerns no one here. The object of education for that mind should be the teaching itself how to react with vigor and economy. What one knows is, in youth, of little moment; they know enough who know how to learn. Only the most energetic, the most highly fitted, and the most favored have overcome the friction, or the viscosity, of inertia, and these were compelled to waste three-fourths of their energy in doing it.

Fit or unfit, Henry Adams stopped his own education in 1871, and began to apply it for practical uses. At the end of twenty years he could sum up the result. He had no complaint to make of man or woman, and had seen little ill-will or dishonesty. He had done as much work as his neighbors would ever stop to look at; artists and writers of his generation had tried, in their way, to hold the standard up; and he, with Clarence King and John Hay, had led a modest existence, filling social gaps where the class was thin. He had enjoyed life amazingly; but he was tired, his nervous energy ran low; he quitted the race-course, left the stable, and sought pastures as far as possible from the old. Education had ended in 1871; life was complete in 1890; the rest mattered so little.

In January, 1892, he found himself in London, alone, in hospital, under a familiar black fog. The coal-fire smelt homelike; the fog tasted of youth; the bed was a world. He had just crawled up from the South Seas with John La Farge, and would rather have gone back to sleep forever in the trade-winds under the southern stars; but companions are rare animals. Paris and London seemed to him fantastic; art strained to be original; and when La Farge asked whether there might not still be room for something simple in art, Adams shook his head: the world was no longer simple and could not express itself simply. He went home as a horse goes back to his stable, because he knew nowhere else to go.

Home was Washington. When Grant’s administration ended, and Evarts came to the Department of State, Adams returned there; presently John Hay came to write the Life of Lincoln; by 1884 they had built adjoining houses on La Fayette Square. To this manger he must turn again. Never did he make a decision more reluctantly. The world since 1871 had been smooth; his friends had died or disappeared; society had grown, yet counted him less; politics had become less social; no one in society had the ear of Government, and no one in Government saw reason to consult society.

After a dreary January in Paris, he drifted to Yorkshire for a week’s rest, and on February 3 took the Teutonic down the Irish Channel. He had not seen an ocean steamer of the new type. To eat one’s dinner through a week of winter gales was a miracle; to have a deck-stateroom with air, and to read by electric light, was more wonder than life had yet supplied. As the Niagara was to the Teutonic—as 1860 was to 1890—so the Teutonic and 1890 must be to the next term—and then? Western Europe might double scale and speed indefinitely without passing bounds; America set the conundrum.

Fate was kind. Rudyard Kipling, on his wedding trip, dashed over him his exuberant fountain of gaiety and wit, as though playing a garden hose on a thirsty and faded begonia. Yet, in the delight, one felt again that the Englishman and the American were not one but two. Clarence King used to say it was due to discord between the wave-lengths of the man-atoms. Perhaps genius soars; perhaps the type divides; all through life one had seen the American on his literary knees to the European, and the European patronize the American; Kipling neither snubbed nor patronized; he would have been first to feel what one meant.

In Washington, society and Government held each other aloof. A presidential election approached; the candidates balanced each other so evenly that the scales scarce moved. Mr. Harrison was an excellent President; yet Adams felt a shade of preference for Mr. Cleveland, because the Democrats represented to him the last remnants of the eighteenth century—the sole remaining protestants against a banker’s Olympus that had ruled Esop’s frog-empire for five-and-twenty years. One might no longer croak except to vote for King Log, or—failing storks—for Grover Cleveland; and even then could not be sure where King Banker lurked behind. King and Hay were loyal Republicans from conviction and habit; to Adams a Western Democrat or a Western Republican seemed actually the same man; to Hay the difference was that of being respectable or not.

Since 1879, King, Hay, and Adams had kept step, shunning public office. With effort their friends had united the Surveys and placed King at the head; he organized, then resigned, to seek his fortune in the West. Hay had served as Assistant Secretary and resigned to write Lincoln. Adams had held no office. No President ever asked him to fill one. The Government required candidates to offer; the Executive consented or refused; an intimate promoted to power commonly sent the courteous Southern message of Lamar: “Of course Mr. Adams knows that anything in my power is at his service.” A la disposicion de Usted! A bow and a conventional smile closed the subject forever. Outsiders who neither wrote for newspapers nor made campaign speeches, who subscribed no funds and entered the White House seldom, placed themselves outside usefulness, and knew it. In fifty years no President asked Adams to cross the square.

Hay stood apart. Republican leaders used his services and took his money with a freedom that staggered even a hardened observer; they never needed him in equivalent office. He seemed to like to be used; in politics this sort of good-nature demands supernatural patience. He liked to play at making Presidents, and laughed at the Presidents he helped to make, and at himself for laughing. Perhaps Adams’s irritation at Mr. Harrison’s manner of dealing his cards made him welcome Mr. Cleveland back to the White House.

Everywhere was slack-water. Both friends had finished their literary work; the redeeming energy of Americans showed signs of check; far off in the Pacific, paralysis crept; silver and exchange loomed; credit shook. Theirs was the highest known success—if it were success—and one asked what it was worth. Old corps commanders tottered to their cards in La Fayette Square; “There goes old Boutwell gambolling like the gambolling kid!” Consideration had value, but hardly so much as five—or ten—thousand a year. The artist stood best; wealth was judge. Hay’s ten years on Lincoln perhaps profited Lincoln more than Hay; Adams’s Jefferson and Madison cost him more than a racing-stable and returned nothing but three readers—Hewitt, McVeagh, and Hay. The world was good-natured and glad to be amused, but that was not consideration, still less power.

Americans, too, had lost the sense of worship. The idea that they worshipped money seemed a delusion; they wasted it more recklessly than any court aristocracy; had no sense of relative values; knew not what to do with it, except use it to make more, or throw it away. West of the Alleghenies the whole country might have been swept clean and replaced within a year or two. The mind, deflected by its pursuit, shunned ideals, distrusted them, and stood alone for its ignorance of the past.

His first step, on returning, took him to Rock Creek to see the bronze figure St. Gaudens had made. Every line and touch interested him; never did he question its meaning. From the Egyptian Sphinx to the Kamakura Daibuts; from Prometheus to Christ; from Michael Angelo to Shelley, art had wrought on this eternal figure. The interest lay in the response of the observer. Tourists came and wanted a meaning; most took it for a portrait; the remnant were vacant-minded without a guide. The clergy taught a deeper lesson. Fascinated by their own reflection, they broke out passionately against what they felt in the figure—despair, atheism, denial. Like the others, the priest saw only what he brought. St. Gaudens held up the mirror and no more. The American layman had lost sight of ideals; the American priest had lost sight of faith.

One active interest absorbed the country: the railway system. Coal output of 160,000,000 tons neared Britain’s 180,000,000; the historian held his breath at the nearness of the crossing. Yet the system, incomplete though it was, seemed to satisfy wants; nothing new was to be learned there; the world hurried to telephones, bicycles, electric trams. At past fifty, Adams solemnly and painfully learned to ride the bicycle.

Nothing else offered itself. He lingered till July; passed the summer on the Deeside; in October returned to Washington and there awaited the reëlection of Mr. Cleveland, which led to no deeper thought than that of taking up some small notes that happened to be outstanding. He had seen enough of the world to be a coward, and above all had an uneasy distrust of bankers.
